title: Neuropol typeface
lede: Ray Larabie’s wide, rounded-square techno face, first given away as freeware in 1996 and widely used in the years around 2000.
summary: Very wide techno sans-serif built from rounded squares, with cut horizontal strokes. Ray Larabie, 1996.

source.label: Typodermic Fonts: Public domain fonts, Neuropol

evidence.note: Inspected Typodermic’s specimen image for Neuropol (1800 × 160) from its public-domain page, and the specimen for its chrome variant Neurochrome (1352 × 120).

styles.note: Clear: the wide techno type of the grammar, made in the period and spread as free software. Its companion Neurochrome renders the same letters as 3D chrome.

context: Typodermic dates Neuropol to 1996 and says the design was influenced by Brendel Type Studio’s Digital Sans (1974). Its sister face Neurochrome (1997) was Neuropol “rendered in Lightwave, a 3D modeling program, applying extrusion, beveling, and reflections to make it look like chrome”. [Typodermic: Public domain fonts](https://typodermicfonts.com/public-domain/#neuropol).

Fonts In Use calls Neuropol “a wide, starkly futuristic typeface” based on rounded squares, like the earlier techno fonts Microgramma, Digital, and Chimes; it was redrawn as Neuropol X in 2004. [Fonts In Use: Neuropol](https://fontsinuse.com/typefaces/175126/neuropol).

Larabie released his Larabie Fonts freeware from 1996. A modified Neuropol was used in the wordmark of the 2006 Winter Olympics in Turin. [Wikipedia: Ray Larabie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ray_Larabie).
observed: The letters are very wide and low. Round letters such as C, D, and O are built from rounded rectangles with straight sides.
Stroke ends are cut flat; the horizontal strokes of E and F stop short of the stem ends and look like separate bars.
The A is a pointed triangle without a crossbar at the apex, and the lowercase a, b, c, d, and e repeat the rounded-rectangle bowl.
Strokes have one even weight, and spacing is generous.
In the Neurochrome specimen the same forms are extruded and bevelled, with black-and-white reflections that read as chrome.
interpretation: Neuropol is the Y2K techno heading face in its free, amateur-web form. Its spread through freeware explains why the wide rounded-square look was everywhere around 2000, on game menus, club flyers, and personal websites.
Neurochrome shows the typical Y2K move of turning a flat face into a 3D chrome render.
borrow: Set short headings in a wide rounded-square face, uppercase, with extra letter spacing.
For a hero word, add a chrome treatment: a vertical silver gradient with a hard highlight line near the middle.

images.alt: Typeface specimen in black on white: the letters A B C D E F and a b c d e set in Neuropol, very wide letters built from rounded rectangles with flat cut stroke ends.
images.caption: Neuropol specimen from [Typodermic Fonts’ public-domain page](https://typodermicfonts.com/public-domain/#neuropol), resized. The font is dedicated to the public domain under CC0 1.0.

rights.statement: Typodermic states that Neuropol and its other early fonts are “released under the official CC0 1.0 Universal public-domain dedication, with no rights reserved”. The stored specimen image shows only the font’s glyphs and comes from the same public-domain page.
